confirmed: Read the complete local markdown (lines 1-271) and extracted text from all 10 PDF pages. The document is the published Proceedings of the Design Society, Volume 5: ICED25 article, printed pp. 409-418, DOI 10.1017/pds.2025.10055, by Vanessa Sattele and Juan Carlos Ortiz; source.version, title, authors and page count agree (PDF pp. 1-10).

The paper reports one facilitated exploratory workshop. It explicitly states: "Each group was assigned a particular AI in each phase in a random manner, regardless of the discipline (designers and architects)." Team-level assignment to AI configurations and expert evaluation of participants' outputs support has_randomized_people_study=true and lab_rct under the codebook (PDF p. 3, printed p. 411, section 3.1; PDF p. 4, printed p. 412, sections 3.3 and 4).

The workshop sample is 19 students, comprising 11 male and 8 female participants aged 19-38, organized into 8 teams: 5 teams of 2 and 3 teams of 3. These are people and teams, respectively, rather than ratings or ideas; the form reproduces these numbers correctly (PDF p. 3, printed p. 411, sections 3.1 and 3.3).

Every team presented a final concept and the results were evaluated. The reported workshop sample of 19 therefore underlies the evaluated outputs; the form correctly notes that the paper gives no separate randomized count, separate analysis sample, exclusions, or people counts for named AI configurations, and leaves allocation and arm counts null (PDF pp. 3-4, printed pp. 411-412, sections 3.1, 3.3 and 4).

All eight assigned tool combinations match Table 1: team 1 Claude/Dall-e; team 2 Gemini/Vizcom; team 3 Gemini/Firefly; team 4 ChatGPT/Firefly; team 5 ChatGPT/KREA.AI; team 6 ChatGPT/Meta; team 7 Claude/Leonardo; team 8 ChatGPT/Leonardo. The prose additionally names Dall-E3, and some teams later switched tools (PDF p. 4, printed p. 412, section 3.3 and Table 1; PDF p. 6, printed p. 414, section 4).

The task was to minimize garbage production in a domestic environment. The workshop lasted two hours; research, concept creation and concept development each lasted 20 minutes, with 5 minutes allocated to each team's final presentation (PDF p. 3, printed p. 411, sections 3.1 and 3.3).

The sole reported outcome entry and the one-line finding accurately describe evaluation of overall creativity by two design experts using CAT, considering problem framing, similarity to existing ideas and context specificity. The authors describe solutions as obvious and generic; no numerical creativity scores, standard errors, confidence intervals or statistical comparisons between AI configurations are printed (PDF p. 4, printed p. 412, section 4; remaining Results on PDF pp. 5-8, printed pp. 413-416).

Core exclusion and context_class="none" are supported: the randomized workshop has only 19 people, below the codebook's 50-person minimum. All teams received AI tools; a no-AI control is proposed for future validation, not reported as a completed second study (PDF pp. 3-4, printed pp. 411-412, sections 3.1 and 3.3; PDF p. 9, printed p. 417, section 5; creativity-codebook.md, sections 3-4).

This is an original workshop study, not a synthesis; the empty synthesis fields are appropriate. The file contains no appendix, and no supplementary material is identified, so supplement.exists="not_stated" is supported (PDF pp. 1-10; sections 3-6 and References).
summary: The form correctly identifies a randomized workshop with 19 students in eight teams and expert evaluation of AI-assisted final concepts, excluded from the core for having fewer than 50 participants. Two outcome fields are incomplete: AI availability should be "yes" and timing "immediate".
